issues.legal_issue: Possession obtained before an urgent acquisition notification, even if initially obtained without lawful authority, becomes possession under the acquisition process and results in the land vesting in the government after the prescribed notice period.
material_facts: Possession of land including the respondent’s land was taken before the acquisition notifications, and the record did not disclose the authority for taking it.
The government later issued an urgent-acquisition notification and notices to interested persons, and the prescribed period after notice expired.
issues.conclusion: On expiry of the prescribed period after publication of the notice, the earlier possession was deemed to be possession under the urgent acquisition process, and the land vested in the government free from encumbrances despite the earlier possession having been obtained unlawfully.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 17(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, when possession is taken following the required notice in an urgent acquisition, the land vests in the government free from encumbrances. Where possession was previously obtained, it is deemed to be possession under that provision when the prescribed period expires. The court applied this principle to the facts; it did not rely on an earlier case for this holding.

rule.if: land_acquisition_case and urgent_acquisition_notification_issued and notice_period_expired and prior_possession_taken

predicates.land_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns the acquisition of land by the government.
predicates.urgent_acquisition_notification_issued: The government issued a notification invoking an urgent process for acquiring the land.
predicates.notice_period_expired: The prescribed period following notice to interested persons expired.
predicates.prior_possession_taken: Possession of the land had been taken before the prescribed period expired.

issues.definition: When land is being acquired through an urgent process, an issued notification, expired notice period, and prior possession together mean that the land vests in the government free from encumbrances.

issues.legal_issue: The government cannot cancel or withdraw an acquisition after the land has vested in it through an urgent acquisition process so as to make the land revert to its former owner.
material_facts: The urgent-acquisition notification and notice process had reached the point at which the land vested in the government.
After that vesting, the government published an order cancelling the acquisition notifications.
The respondent sought to have the cancellation quashed and the acquisition-related duties performed.
issues.conclusion: The government could not cancel or withdraw the notifications after the land had vested, and cancellation could not cause the land to revert to the original owner.
issues.legal_principle: Section 48(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, permits withdrawal from acquisition only where possession has not been taken. Although section 21 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, permits cancellation or rescission of notifications under sections 4 and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, that general power cannot be used after statutory vesting under section 17(1). The court referred to State of Madhya Pradesh v. Vishnu Prasad Sharma, explaining that its observations supported the conclusion that notifications could not be cancelled after possession under section 17(1) and vesting.

predicates.land_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns the government’s acquisition of land.
predicates.land_has_vested: The land has vested in the government through the acquisition process.
predicates.government_attempts_to_cancel_or_withdra: The government attempts to cancel the acquisition or withdraw from it after vesting.

issues.definition: In a land acquisition, if the land has vested and the government then attempts to cancel or withdraw the acquisition, that attempt cannot reverse the vesting.

issues.legal_issue: The government may not raise for the first time on appeal that an urgent acquisition was unauthorized because the land was not waste or arable when it did not raise that ground before the court below.
material_facts: The government issued a notification invoking the urgent acquisition power, which could be exercised only for waste or arable land.
The notification did not state that the land was waste or arable.
The government had not contended before the Judicial Commissioner that the land was not waste or arable or that the notification was unauthorized, but raised that contention on appeal.
issues.conclusion: It was not open to the government to contend for the first time on appeal that the land was not waste or arable and that the urgent-acquisition notification was unauthorized.
issues.legal_principle: The court stated that the powers under sections 17(1) and 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, may be exercised only when the land is waste or arable. Because the government had not challenged the notification on that ground before the Judicial Commissioner, it could not raise the contention for the first time on appeal. No earlier case was relied on for this holding.

predicates.appeal_from_acquisition_writ_order: The proceeding is an appeal from an order on a writ petition concerning a land acquisition.
predicates.urgent_acquisition_power_invoked: The government invoked an urgent acquisition power that is available only for land meeting a specified eligibility condition.
predicates.eligibility_ground_not_raised_below: The government did not argue before the court below that the land failed the eligibility condition.

issues.definition: In an appeal from a writ order concerning an urgent acquisition, if the government invoked a power subject to an eligibility condition but did not dispute eligibility below, it cannot raise that ground for the first time on appeal.
